reasons: Quote ids are built into SQL text with quote escaping, not safe parameters.
Misses and round-trip failures are only logged, so bad rows are not blocked.
Tests and scripts are referred to in comments but are not part of this file.
Positions must match the database count exactly, which depends on other modules.

terms.meaning: One whole character, where an emoji or some symbols count as one even though JavaScript may count them as two.
JavaScript's internal unit for text, where some characters take two units.
A position number counting from the start of the text, used to cut out a piece.
A stored start and end position in a document that marks one quote.
Cleaning text so small differences such as case, curly quotes, and spacing do not stop a match.
A fixed-length fingerprint of text; the same text always gives the same fingerprint.
Anything that can run database statements, so tests can supply their own.
Storing a value, then reading it back from the database to confirm it matches.
The database function that cuts out text between two positions.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Module purpose and single anchorer
sections.what: Explains this file is the one place that finds quote positions in stored pages. Sets the minimum quote length to 8 characters.
sections.why: The header says a second copy of this logic would bring back the offset bug.
sections.watch_out: Other code must import from this file, since a second copy reintroduces the bug.

sections.name: cpIndexMap
sections.title: Character position lookup table
sections.what: Builds a table that converts a JavaScript text position into a count of whole characters, where an emoji counts as one.
sections.why: The comments say the database counts characters while JavaScript counts half-units for some symbols, so a conversion is needed.
sections.watch_out: The table has one entry per text unit, so very large documents use a lot of memory.

sections.name: charLengthOf
sections.title: Counting characters the database way
sections.what: Returns the number of whole characters in a text.
sections.why: The comment says it matches the database length function, unlike the plain JavaScript length.
sections.watch_out: Use this rather than plain length whenever a size is stored, or sizes will disagree with the database.

sections.name: hashText
sections.title: Fingerprint of stored text
sections.what: Returns a SHA-256 fingerprint of a text, used to tell whether two stored pages hold the same content.
sections.why: The persist comment says the fingerprint is over extracted text, because offsets index into that text.
sections.watch_out: Two pages with the same text but different layout get the same fingerprint.

sections.name: NormMap
sections.title: Cleaned text with position map
sections.what: Describes a structure holding cleaned text plus a map back to each character's original position.
sections.why: The comment says matches are found in cleaned text and must point back to the original.
sections.watch_out: The text and its map must stay in step; changing one without the other breaks positions.

sections.name: normalizeWithMap
sections.title: Cleaning text while tracking positions
sections.what: Lowercases text, changes curly quotes to straight ones and dash variants to a plain hyphen, and collapses runs of whitespace to one space, while recording each kept character's original position.
sections.why: The comment says it produces exactly what the shared text cleaner produces, plus the position map.
sections.watch_out: It must match the shared text cleaner exactly; if they drift apart, matches fail without any error.

sections.name: Doc
sections.title: Document in two position systems
sections.what: Bundles the stored text, its character list, its position table, and its cleaned version into one object.
sections.why: The comment says callers anchor against exactly the text that was stored.
sections.watch_out: The bundle must be built from the same text that was saved to the database.

sections.name: buildDoc
sections.title: Building the document bundle
sections.what: Takes stored text and builds the full bundle described above.
sections.why: A single builder keeps every caller using the same setup.
sections.watch_out: Building from different text than was stored would give wrong positions.

sections.name: sliceCp
sections.title: Cutting out a quote by characters
sections.what: Returns the characters between a start and end position, so the stored quote equals what the database would cut.
sections.why: The comment says the stored quote must match the database slice.
sections.watch_out: Positions here are character positions, not JavaScript positions.

sections.name: MatchHit
sections.title: A located match
sections.what: Describes one match: start and end positions, the method that found it, and its score.
sections.why: Records how the match was found and how much to trust it.
sections.watch_out: Start is included and end is excluded, so mixing these up shifts the quote by one.

sections.name: SCORES
sections.title: Confidence score for each method
sections.what: Gives each match method a score: exact 1, normalized 0.95, first ten words 0.7, figure only 0.3.
sections.why: Likely reason: ranks how strong a match is so weak matches can be seen as weak.
sections.watch_out: Scores are saved with each match, so changing them does not update old rows.

sections.name: STRONG_METHODS
sections.title: Methods counted as real proof
sections.what: Lists the methods that count as strong: exact and normalized matches, including the fragment forms. First ten words and figure-only matches are excluded.
sections.why: The comment explains a first ten words match can succeed while the quote tail is invented, and figure matches inflated coverage.
sections.watch_out: Adding first ten words here would let wrong quotes count as correct.

sections.name: isStrong
sections.title: Checking if a method is strong
sections.what: Returns true when a method name is in the strong list.
sections.why: A single check keeps callers from repeating the list.
sections.watch_out: Unknown method names return false, so new methods count as weak until listed.

sections.name: exactHit
sections.title: Exact text search
sections.what: Searches the stored text for the quote exactly as written, if it is long enough, and converts the position to characters.
sections.why: The comment says the plain search works in JavaScript units, so the result must be converted.
sections.watch_out: Quotes under 8 characters are rejected.

sections.name: rawRangeFromNorm
sections.title: Converting cleaned positions to raw
sections.what: Turns a range in the cleaned text into the matching range in the original text.
sections.why: Matches are found in cleaned text, but the stored positions must refer to the original.
sections.watch_out: Returns nothing for an empty or reversed range, so callers must handle that.

sections.name: normHit
sections.title: Search after cleaning text
sections.what: Cleans the quote the same way as the document, searches the cleaned text, and maps the result back.
sections.why: Lets a quote match despite case, curly quotes, or spacing differences.
sections.watch_out: Cleaning must happen the same way on both sides, or matches silently fail.

sections.name: first10Hit
sections.title: Search on first ten words
sections.what: If the quote has more than ten words, searches only for its first ten words.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the comments, which mark it as weak evidence.
sections.watch_out: A first ten words match must never be treated as verified quote text.

sections.name: numericHit
sections.title: Search for a figure
sections.what: Picks the longest number in the quote with at least two digits and checks that it appears on the page.
sections.why: Lets the system show that a figure appears somewhere, even if the surrounding text is not found.
sections.watch_out: This only proves the figure is present, not that the quote is right.

sections.name: locate
sections.title: Trying match methods in order
sections.what: Tries the fragment exact match, then the fragment cleaned match, then exact, cleaned, first ten words, and figures. Stops at the first success.
sections.why: Strictest first, so the best available match is the one recorded.
sections.watch_out: The order is important; reordering would record weaker matches in place of stronger ones.

sections.name: ACCEPTANCE_LEVELS, AcceptanceLevel
sections.title: Strictness levels for quote checks
sections.what: Lists five tolerance levels from strictest to loosest: exact, normalized, punctuation tolerant, whitespace insensitive, and footnote insertion.
sections.why: The comment says the order is the order the checker tries them, and a tighter rule should be recorded when several apply.
sections.watch_out: The order drives which label is recorded, so changing it changes stored labels.

sections.name: REJECTED_LEVELS
sections.title: Looser rule deliberately excluded
sections.what: Records a rule that was tried and rejected: keeping only letters and digits.
sections.why: The comment says it accepted made-up quotes such as label and value pairs, which an audit found.
sections.watch_out: Do not add it to the accepted levels; the comment says it was tested and rejected.

sections.name: PUNCT
sections.title: Punctuation characters list
sections.what: Lists the punctuation marks that count when deciding whether a space sits next to punctuation.
sections.why: Reason not stated beyond the comment. It defines which spacing differences are tolerated.
sections.watch_out: Punctuation not in this list keeps its spacing, so those quotes will not match at that level.

sections.name: rangeFromNormMap
sections.title: Mapping cleaned range to raw
sections.what: Converts a range in a looser text view into character positions in the original text.
sections.why: Each looser view still needs to point back to the original text.
sections.watch_out: Returns nothing when the mapped range is empty.

sections.name: deriveVariant, dropAllSpaces
sections.title: Looser text views
sections.what: Builds a copy of the cleaned text with some characters removed while keeping pointers to the original. One version removes every space.
sections.why: Lets matches survive line breaks and split table cells, as the comment explains.
sections.watch_out: The quote must be reduced in exactly the same way, or no match is found.

sections.name: dropSpaceByPunct
sections.title: Dropping spaces beside punctuation
sections.what: Removes a space only when it sits next to one of the listed punctuation marks.
sections.why: Lets a quote with a space before a full stop match the page without that space. No letter or digit is removed.
sections.watch_out: Decimal points are kept, so 6.5 correctly cannot match 65.

sections.name: variantText
sections.title: Applying the same drop rule
sections.what: Removes the same characters from the quote as the drop rule removes from the page.
sections.why: Keeps the quote and page in the same form before comparing.
sections.watch_out: The drop rule used here must be the same one used for the page text.

sections.name: Tok
sections.title: One word token
sections.what: Holds a word in comparison form plus its start and end positions in the cleaned text.
sections.why: Needed for the footnote-tolerant search, which compares word by word.
sections.watch_out: Positions here are in cleaned characters, not the original text.

sections.name: tokenForm
sections.title: Comparison form of a word
sections.what: Removes bracketed reference numbers such as [12] or (3), then trims punctuation from the start and end of the word.
sections.why: The comment says footnote markers are often attached to the word before them.
sections.watch_out: Only markers of one to three digits are removed, so longer numbers in brackets stay.

sections.name: tokenizeNorm
sections.title: Splitting document into words
sections.what: Splits the cleaned page text into word tokens, each with its position, skipping empty ones.
sections.why: Needed so the footnote search can compare the page and quote one word at a time.
sections.watch_out: Words are split only on single spaces, which matches the cleaned text.

sections.name: tokenizePlain
sections.title: Splitting quote into words
sections.what: Splits the quote on spaces and applies the same comparison form to each word.
sections.why: So the quote and page are compared the same way.
sections.watch_out: Only literal spaces split words.

sections.name: isSkippableDocToken
sections.title: Document words that may be skipped
sections.what: Allows the search to skip a page word that is all digits or three characters or fewer.
sections.why: The comment says these are typical footnote markers.
sections.watch_out: Short real words can also be skipped, so the rule is looser than its name suggests.

sections.name: AcceptanceHit
sections.title: Result of a quote check
sections.what: Holds the tolerance level reached and the raw start and end positions.
sections.why: Records which rule explained the match.
sections.watch_out: Positions here are raw character positions.

sections.name: findAcceptance (part 1)
sections.title: Checking quote is on page
sections.what: Tries each tolerance level in order and returns the first that matches, or nothing if none does. Quotes under 8 characters are rejected.
sections.why: The comment says it exists so a quote is checked against the page before it is stored.
sections.watch_out: A nothing result is the signal to refuse the write, and callers must act on it.

sections.name: findAcceptance: for
sections.title: Footnote-tolerant word search
sections.what: Looks for every quote word in order, allowing only short or numeric page words to appear between them, up to four skips. Needs at least three quote words.
sections.why: The comment says it tolerates footnote markers but never an invented clause.
sections.watch_out: It checks every possible start, so very long pages with many repeats are slower.

sections.name: Executor
sections.title: Database runner type
sections.what: Describes anything able to run database statements, defaulting to the main database connection.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets tests and scripts pass their own connection.
sections.watch_out: The runner must accept the same statement form used here.

sections.name: CapturedPage
sections.title: Captured page contents
sections.what: Describes one fetched page: its URL, extracted text, optional title and publisher, how it was retrieved, and its status and size.
sections.why: The comment says the extracted text is exactly what the offsets point into.
sections.watch_out: The text must not be edited after capture, or positions become wrong.

sections.name: persistDocument
sections.title: Saving page text once
sections.what: Saves the page as a document, or reuses an existing copy with the same URL and fingerprint. Returns the document id and the built bundle.
sections.why: The comment says the fingerprint is over extracted text, not raw bytes.
sections.watch_out: Duplicate detection needs the URL to match exactly, so URL variants create separate copies.

sections.name: AnchorOutcome
sections.title: Result of anchoring one quote
sections.what: Describes the outcome for one quote: whether it was anchored, whether the match is strong, the method, positions, and stored quote.
sections.why: Lets callers report results and count them.
sections.watch_out: Empty values mean no span was written.

sections.name: anchorQuote
sections.title: Writing the span for a quote
sections.what: Finds the quote; if found, saves its span and marks the evidence as span anchored. If not found, writes nothing and reports the miss.
sections.why: The comment says a miss is a defect, not a legacy case, so it is never classified that way.
sections.watch_out: The evidence status is set on every successful call, even when the span already existed.

sections.name: RoundTripResult
sections.title: Database check result type
sections.what: Describes the result of the database check: totals, passes, and a list of failures showing stored and database text.
sections.why: Reason not stated beyond its fields. It reports the acceptance test.
sections.watch_out: A failure list with differing texts is the evidence to read first.

sections.name: verifySpansInSql
sections.title: Database check of spans
sections.what: Asks the database to cut each stored span from its document and compares the result with the stored quote. Can be limited to a list of evidence ids, or cover everything.
sections.why: The comment says the database is the referee, so the writer and checker cannot share one mistake.
sections.watch_out: Evidence ids are pasted into the query text with quote doubling, so unusual ids need care.

sections.name: CaptureAnchorStats
sections.title: Counts for an anchoring run
sections.what: Describes the counts recorded for one run: rows considered, documents saved, spans, strong anchors, misses, misses whose quote is absent, rows with no document, and round-trip results.
sections.why: The comment says these counts reach the run record.
sections.watch_out: A miss with the quote absent points to a text extraction problem, not a matching problem.

sections.name: EMPTY_ANCHOR_STATS
sections.title: Blank starting counts
sections.what: Holds a set of zero counts used as the starting values for each run.
sections.why: So every run starts clean.
sections.watch_out: The code copies this object before changing it, so it must not be edited in place.

sections.name: EvidenceToAnchor
sections.title: Input row for anchoring
sections.what: Describes what each evidence row must supply: its id, quote text, URL, and optional fragment.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond its fields.
sections.watch_out: A missing URL makes the row count as having no document.

sections.name: canonicalUrl
sections.title: Standard form of web address
sections.what: Removes the part after a hash, lowercases the scheme and host, and removes a trailing slash except on the root. Returns the input unchanged if it cannot be parsed.
sections.why: The comment says one page should be fetched and stored once, even if addresses differ slightly.
sections.watch_out: Paths are kept as they are, since they can be case-sensitive.

sections.name: anchorCapturedEvidence (part 1)
sections.title: Anchoring new evidence against pages
sections.what: For a batch of new evidence rows, finds each row's page by standard URL. Describes the batch processing rules and that it never throws.
sections.why: The comment says anchoring records and reports; it does not block the write path.
sections.watch_out: Misses do not stop anything, so they only appear in logs and statistics.

sections.name: anchorCapturedEvidence: if
sections.title: Saving pages and anchoring quotes
sections.what: Saves each page once per batch, logging any failure. Anchors each quote. On a miss, checks whether the quote text is present anywhere and logs those facts.
sections.why: The comment says the log states facts and leaves classification to the reader.
sections.watch_out: Failures are logged as warnings only, so bad quotes can still be kept.

sections.name: anchorCapturedEvidence: if
sections.title: Round-trip check and summary
sections.what: Runs the database check on the anchored rows, logs each failure, and prints a summary with the strong-anchor rate over all evidence written.
sections.why: The comment says the headline uses evidence written as the denominator, so a low anchoring rate cannot hide behind a high rate.
sections.watch_out: If the database check throws, only a warning is logged and the round-trip counts stay at zero.

summary: Finds where each quote sits inside a stored copy of its source text, and records the start and end positions in the database so the quote can be checked later.
purpose: Lets the app prove that a quote really appears in its source, and point to the exact place. It is the single shared place for this logic, so the writer and the checker agree on what 'present on the page' means.
why: The header says a second copy of this logic caused an offset bug. It also says a quote must be checked against the page before it is stored, because 442 unlocatable quotes were written earlier.
how: 1. `buildDoc` makes a stored text that has a character list, a position lookup, and a cleaned version. 2. `locate` tries match methods from strictest to loosest and stops at the first hit. 3. `findAcceptance` is a separate checker that tries five tolerance levels and returns nothing if none fit. 4. `persistDocument` saves page text once, keyed by URL and content hash. 5. `anchorQuote` saves the span and marks the evidence as span anchored. 6. `anchorCapturedEvidence` runs these steps for a batch and logs misses. 7. `verifySpansInSql` asks the database to cut each span and compares it with the stored quote.
inputs: Stored or fetched page text with its URL. Evidence rows with a quote (verbatim), an optional fragment, and a URL. A database connection, used through an executor.
outputs: Rows in source_document and source_span. The evidence table's provenance class is set to span anchored. Counts and warnings in logs and a statistics object. A round-trip result listing any mismatches.
risks: Quote ids are pasted into a SQL text string with quote doubling rather than passed as safe parameters. Misses are only logged, so bad quotes can still be stored. The function never throws for a bad batch, so problems can pass unnoticed unless someone reads logs or stats. Offsets are character positions, so any change to text cleaning shifts every stored position.
debug: Read the ANCHOR MISS log lines: they say whether the quote text is present in the stored text and at which level. If the round-trip check fails, the log prints the stored quote and the database slice side by side. If stats show many no-document cases, check canonicalUrl output matches the stored URL. Compare normalizeWithMap with normalizeText if matches fail unexpectedly.
